title: Verb + object + to: I want you to come
tagline: After want, ask, tell and friends, put the person first and then 'to' + verb — never 'that'.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Writing Part 2 — email or letter: asking and telling people to do things
why: When you want somebody else to do something, English puts that person straight after the verb and links the action with to: I want you to come. Learners often copy the Spanish 'quiero que vengas' pattern and write want that you come, which is always wrong. This frame turns up in key word transformations, in open cloze gaps and in every email where you ask for help or give instructions.

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: Miss Vega expects us to hand in the essay on Monday.
Liam reminded Sofia to bring her passport.
The school allows students to use tablets in class.
The guide told us not to feed the animals.
Her dad let her borrow the car.
We were made to run an extra lap.
Visitors are asked to switch off their phones.

use.point: Wishes and expectations about other people: want, would like, expect

examples.text: My parents want me to take a gap year before university.
Sofia would like her cousin to visit Cusco with her.
examples.note: would like is more polite and more formal than want

examples.text: The organisers expect every team to arrive an hour early.
examples.note: expect = think that someone will, or should

use.point: Telling, asking and persuading: ask, tell, remind, warn, persuade, encourage

examples.text: Nadia asked Mateo to lend her his notes.
The lifeguard warned the swimmers not to go beyond the red flags.
examples.note: negative: not to, placed before the verb

examples.text: Miss Vega encouraged Liam to enter the writing competition.
It took an hour, but Sofia persuaded her mum to let her go to the concert.
examples.note: persuade = succeed in convincing; the result happens

use.point: make and let: no 'to' after the object

examples.text: Mateo's dad let him stay up for the match.

use.point: The passive: be asked, be told, be allowed, be made

examples.text: Candidates are asked to put their phones in the box.
We weren't allowed to take photos inside the museum.

watch_out.wrong: I want that you come to my party.
watch_out.right: I want you to come to my party.
watch_out.why: After want use object + to-infinitive, never a that clause.

watch_out.wrong: She told me to not be late.
watch_out.right: She told me not to be late.
watch_out.why: The negative is not to + infinitive; to not sounds wrong in exam English.

watch_out.wrong: Her dad let her to go out on Friday.
watch_out.right: Her dad let her go out on Friday.
watch_out.why: Let takes the bare infinitive, with no to.

watch_out.wrong: The teacher made us to rewrite the paragraph.
watch_out.right: The teacher made us rewrite the paragraph.
watch_out.why: Make + object + bare infinitive in the active.

watch_out.wrong: We were made rewrite the whole paragraph.
watch_out.right: We were made to rewrite the whole paragraph.
watch_out.why: In the passive, made needs to back again.

watch_out.wrong: Liam told to me to wait outside.
watch_out.why: Tell takes the person directly, with no to before the object.

dialogue.title: A favour before the trip
dialogue.context: Sofia and Mateo are organising a school trip, and Miss Vega is checking the plan.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Mateo, I'd like you to design the poster for the trip.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Sure. Who asked you to organise everything, by the way?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Miss Vega. She wants us to finish the plan by Friday.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That's right. I expect everyone to bring a signed form, so please remind them to hand it in.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: What if somebody forgets? Can we let them join the trip anyway?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: No. I won't allow anyone to travel without one, and I'd rather you didn't make exceptions.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Understood. Liam persuaded his mum to sign hers last night, so he's fine.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I'll encourage the others to send theirs today. I'll tell them not to leave it until Friday.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. And warn them not to bring too much luggage — the bus is small.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Don't worry. We'll make them pack light!

items.sentence: My parents want me ___ a gap year.
The teacher made us ___ the essay again.
items.why: make + object + bare infinitive in the active

items.sentence: Liam's coach warned him ___ late for training.
Sofia would like ___ to the party.
items.why: would like + object + to-infinitive, not a that-clause

items.sentence: We weren't allowed ___ phones in the exam hall.
Miss Vega let the class ___ their own seats.
He persuaded his sister ___ him with the project.
The staff expect students ___ on time.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: Mateo's dad asked him ___ (turn) the music down.
The ending of the film made me ___ (cry).
I'd like you ___ (not/tell) anyone about the surprise.
Nadia reminded us ___ (bring) our swimming kit.
Our teacher encouraged us ___ (read) more in English.
The security guard didn't let anyone ___ (enter) the stadium.
We were told ___ (wait) outside until our names were called.
Sofia's mum wants her ___ (study) harder before the exam.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Mateo's mum said to him, 'Please tidy your room.'
I wish you would stay calm during the interview.
The teacher made us stay behind after the lesson.
'Don't touch the exhibits,' the guide told the children.
My parents allowed me to go to the concert.
'You should apply,' Miss Vega said to Sofia.

summary: Put the person straight after the verb, then to + infinitive: I want you to come, never want that you come.
Ask, tell, remind, warn, persuade, encourage and allow all follow the same object + to-infinitive pattern.
The negative is not to + infinitive: He told me not to be late.
After make and let the infinitive has no to in the active; in the passive, be made gets to back.
Passives such as be asked to, be told to and be allowed to are common in notices and emails.
